transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2027-05-10
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: 42 minutes
Attendees: Sam Rivera (Redwood AE), Maya Chen (Redwood SE), Jon Park (Redwood Solutions), Tom Alvarez (Neptune Eng Mgr), Priya Singh (Neptune SRE), Elena Kors (Neptune Product), Mike O'Neal (Neptune CTO, joined 15:12)

Summary (auto): dry-run prep + burst handoff run through; verify autoscale policies, pre-warm/warmup, expected latency targets and rollback behaviors; plan dry-run next week; share runbook and scripts.

Topics: autoscale policy tuning, burst sizing, KV cache warmup, model fallback variants, SOC2 / audit logs question, next steps dry-run.

Transcript:
[00:00] Sam Rivera: All right everyone, thanks for joining. we are gonna run through the dry-run and handoff for the burst rehearsal, um I think we have most of the key people, Mike you'll join a bit later thanks for tacking on.
[00:18] Tom Alvarez: Yep thanks Sam, Tom here. quick context — our peak window is still the same, roughly 9 to 11 a.m. ET with spikes up to 3.2k qps for short bursts, and we want to make sure Dedicated sizing actually holds latency under 200ms p50 for the critical path.
[00:36] Maya Chen: cool, and just to set expectations, the plan we proposed uses 6 reserved GPUs with a burst pool of two extra nodes and an autoscale policy that scales on token-in-flight and P99 latency. There's also a pre-warm step to populate the KV cache.
[00:52] Priya Singh: quick question — when you say kv cache pre-warm, what's the warm window and how much memory are we talking, because our infra team is sensitive to memory spikes?
[01:08] Maya Chen: yep totally, so the warmup script does prefix loads for the top 100k keys we saw in the pilot logs, that tends to take about 6-8 minutes and uses about 12 to 18GB of GPU-side kv cache on the nvidia A100 equivalents. that's an estimate; depending on model sequence lengths it can vary.
[01:28] Tom Alvarez: 6-8 minutes is OK but we'd like the option to do a rolling warm so we don't blow memory on new nodes. can the script do incremental loading?
[01:36] Maya Chen: absolutely it supports chunked loading, you can pass batch-size and concurrency. the script's in python, we can share in the repo.
[01:44] Elena Kors: I just want to be clear on success criteria: for product, it's p50 under 200ms, p95 under 450ms during burst windows, and no errors above 1% right?
[01:56] Sam Rivera: that's what we have but open to adjust — our suggestion is to aim for p95 < 450ms and error < 0.5% for this dry-run, we'll set automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant if the latency or error SLOs trip.
[02:12] Tom Alvarez: that fallback — does it degrade outputs? we need to understand fidelity tradeoffs for product sign-off.
[02:20] Jon Park: yeah quick note, the fallback picks a quantized variant with slightly higher hallucination risk — in our evals the quality delta was small for the intents Neptune uses, but we'll attach the eval spreadsheet.
[02:32] Priya Singh: and the route for fallback, is it per request or per route? what granularity?
[02:38] Maya Chen: it's route-level for now, you can set per-customer overrides, but the default is per-api-route to keep routing table small.
[02:46] Mike O'Neal: (joined) hey all, sorry for being late, can you recap what we actually will break during the dry-run? I don't want production blips.
[02:56] Sam Rivera: welcome Mike — short answer: the dry-run will be against a shadow environment pointed at a staging model that mirrors production traffic shape; we won't hit production backends, but we will exercise capacity and autoscale rules. hope that helps.
[03:12] Mike O'Neal: good. Priya, what's our rollback comfort?
[03:16] Priya Singh: we want explicit circuit-breakers and an operator quick-toggle, we can't have silent downgrades.
[03:22] Sam Rivera: agreed — the plan includes a manual override in the Console and an automated rollback policy if p99 crosses 600ms for more than two minutes.
[03:30] Tom Alvarez: can you show the autoscale policy conditions?
[03:34] Maya Chen: sure, high level: scale up when token-in-flight > 80k or p99 > 480ms for 60s, scale down after sustained low utilization 10m and p99 < 300ms. burst nodes are pre-provisioned but billed cold unless we attach them. we also have a 'soft-prewarm' that boots nodes sooner but not full warm.
[03:58] Elena Kors: what's the billing implication if we keep burst nodes in warm but idle?
[04:02] Sam Rivera: you'll pay for reserved pool and small keep-alive charges for warm nodes; Redwood Dedicated pricing doc spells it out, we'll attach the line items.
[04:14] Tom Alvarez: about warm nodes — we want to avoid double-charging or ghost GPUs billed while not used. can you guarantee billing visibility?
[04:24] Sam Rivera: yes console shows token-level and node-level charge breakdown, and we'll give access to the usage dashboard for your finance folks.
[04:32] Maya Chen: also small note — the autoscaler uses both capacity and latency signals. some customers have complained about oscillation under spiky traffic; we propose a cooldown window and smoothing via exponential moving average on token-in-flight so we don't thrash.
[04:50] Priya Singh: that makes sense. for the dry-run we want the smoothing to be conservative so we don't under-scale.
[04:56] Maya Chen: we'll set t1 parameters to more aggressive scale-up, conservative scale-down for the dry-run.
[05:04] Tom Alvarez: any thoughts on pre-split routing — like can we route 20% of traffic to a fallback before a full switch?
[05:12] Jon Park: yes we can do canary style, the Console supports percentage rollouts. also our runbook includes a staged rollout playbook: 10% then 30% then 100% with checks between.
[05:22] Elena Kors: during the run I'd like product metrics tied to the runs — not just infra metrics, we need throughput per intent and error rate per intent.
[05:30] Sam Rivera: totally — we'll add intent-level tagging in the dry-run traffic generator so you can slice by intent.
[05:36] Priya Singh: slightly tangential — SOC2 questions: where do logs live, and are they available for audit?
[05:44] Maya Chen: logs are stored in your VPC/private deployment if you choose Private; for Dedicated they're accessible via offsite syslog/S3 with encryption, retention and audit logs are configurable — we have SOC2 and ISO attestation docs, will share link.
[05:58] Tom Alvarez: good. can you remind us about KMS and customer-managed keys?
[06:02] Sam Rivera: yes Redwood supports customer-managed keys (KMS/HSM) for Private and Dedicated with envelope encryption; we can map a key per environment.
[06:10] Mike O'Neal: on the dry-run, how realistic is the model size and quantization? I don't want the test to overpromise.
[06:18] Maya Chen: we'll use the same model version as pilot but with a quantized fallback variant. performance will mirror production within a small margin, but we always call out that synthetic traffic can miss real-world latencies.
[06:32] Tom Alvarez: what about cold-starts for the model itself vs. KV cache — which is the dominant factor?
[06:38] Jon Park: for our architecture the kv-cache and tokenizer warm are the big ones. model load is longer but typically amortized; the runtime keeps models resident in GPU memory for Dedicated pools.
[06:50] Priya Singh: any chance to run a quick synthetic right now? I'm curious about the numbers.
[06:54] Maya Chen: we could run a small 30s spike but won't be meaningful here, better to do the Monday dry-run when we can capture full logs.
[07:02] Tom Alvarez: ok agreed.
[07:04] Sam Rivera: next section, handoff checklist — Maya do you want to run through the runbook?
[07:10] Maya Chen: yes. Step 1: provision reserved pool plus burst nodes; Step 2: prewarm KV via our warmup script (chunked by default); Step 3: start traffic generator on staging and increment to 3k qps over 10 minutes; Step 4: monitor p50/p95/p99 and error rates; Step 5: trigger fallback at threshold and validate outputs; Step 6: rollback and run post-mortem.
[07:34] Priya Singh: the warmup script — will it run as a job in our cluster or as part of the Redwood agent?
[07:40] Maya Chen: it's a standalone python job you can run from any bastion with credentials; for Private we can distribute a containerized runner.
[07:48] Elena Kors: can we have the runbook show screenshots of the Console for the toggles? that's helpful for our ops runbook.
[07:54] Sam Rivera: yep we'll add screenshots and CLI examples.
[07:58] Tom Alvarez: question on capacity math — how did you arrive at 6 reserved GPUs + 2 burst? show the math.
[08:06] Jon Park: we used token-per-second throughput from your production logs, assumed 1.8k tokens per second per GPU baseline at median sequence length, factored headroom for 2x because of concurrency, and then added burst capacity to cover 30% headroom. we'll share the spreadsheet.
[08:24] Tom Alvarez: please share the spreadsheet intact, we need to sanity check.
[08:28] Sam Rivera: will do.
[08:30] Priya Singh: what's the expected time to add a burst node and get it fully warm?
[08:34] Maya Chen: cold-boot to node up is ~90-120s, warm-up to KV ready depends on number of keys, 6-8 minutes typical; total 8-10 minutes for full readiness.
[08:46] Mike O'Neal: that's longer than I'd like, is there any way to reduce the warm time?
[08:50] Jon Park: you can keep a lightweight pre-warmed pool (soft-prewarm) which keeps node kernel and model loaded but not KV fully populated; that reduces warm to under 2m but costs more.
[08:58] Elena Kors: is partial warm safe in terms of correctness?
[09:02] Maya Chen: yes, partial warm serves requests but some prefixes may not hit cache, so p95 could be higher until KV fully warms.
[09:12] Tom Alvarez: then maybe we do soft-prewarm + incremental KV load to balance cost/latency. that's probably our preference.
[09:18] Priya Singh: agree. let's capture that as the run plan.
[09:22] Sam Rivera: captured.
[09:24] Maya Chen: one more operational note — when you run the traffic generator, include backpressure signals from your ingestion pipeline in the seed, otherwise the distribution will be artificially smooth.
[09:36] Tom Alvarez: good call. we'll modify the generator.
[09:40] Elena Kors: can Redwood share a template for the traffic generator config?
[09:44] Maya Chen: yes we'll share the config with examples for ramp, sawtooth spikes, and burst windows.
[09:52] Tom Alvarez: I'd like to talk briefly about metrics retention during the dry-run — our compliance team will ask to keep raw logs for 90 days. is that feasible?
[09:58] Sam Rivera: yes, retention is configurable, but long retention may increase costs; we'll document the storage delta.
[10:06] Priya Singh: anything we should be worried about from the security side during the run? external access, tokens?
[10:12] Maya Chen: we'll issue short-lived creds for the dry-run and recommend using ephemeral keys. plus we can restrict IPs.
[10:18] Tom Alvarez: ok.
[10:20] Sam Rivera: quick aside — competitor note, we saw a few customers moving to other endpoints because they wanted aggressive prewarming baked into pricing; we'll show how our soft-prewarm + usage reporting can be tuned to their needs, not a hard sell.
[10:34] Mike O'Neal: fine, back to runbook, are we capturing the exact rollback steps?
[10:38] Jon Park: yes, rollback playbook includes: toggle to fallback model, scale down burst nodes via console, purge partial KV if needed, and re-run postmortem script to collect metrics. we'll include runbook times.
[10:52] Elena Kors: how do we handle partial failures — say one node flaps during the spike — what's the alerting threshold?
[10:58] Maya Chen: alert on node flaps > 2 in 5 minutes; plus auto-remediate replacing node, if replacement fails for more than 3 attempts we drain and route traffic to fallback.
[11:12] Priya Singh: can we get an SLA for dedicated pool in the pilot? given we are evaluating for production later.
[11:18] Sam Rivera: we can include pilot-level uptime commitments in the contract addendum; for full SLA we move to enterprise Reserved agreements.
[11:26] Tom Alvarez: financially, if we hit a productive burst and exceed reserved capacity, how are overages handled during the POC?
[11:34] Sam Rivera: we'll cap overage and alert you, and for the POC we can agree not to auto-bill without signoff; we'll, like, predefine a commit or an overage cap.
[11:44] Mike O'Neal: good.
[11:46] Sam Rivera: okay final section — dry-run schedule and owners. proposed dry-run start: Monday 2027-05-17 at 09:00 ET; Prep window Friday for scripts and prewarm; Redwood SE to be on-call during run plus an on-call number.
[12:04] Tom Alvarez: works for us, set it up.
[12:08] Elena Kors: we want a debrief 2 hours after the run finishes.
[12:12] Priya Singh: and attach all logs to the shared S3 for analysis.
[12:16] Sam Rivera: will do.
[12:18] Maya Chen: action items recap — I'll share warmup script and autoscale templates; Sam will share runbook and cost spreadsheet; Tom/Priya will run the generator and upload logs.
[12:32] Tom Alvarez: small nit — in the runbook can you include CLI snippets for emergency rollback? our ops prefers CLI toggles.
[12:38] Jon Park: yes CLI and UI both.
[12:42] Elena Kors: anything else on compliance?
[12:46] Priya Singh: just please ensure audit logs are on and accessible.
[12:50] Sam Rivera: noted.
[12:52] Mike O'Neal: one last question — if dry-run shows a 20% higher p95 than expected, what do we do?
[12:58] Maya Chen: we'd immediately trigger canary fallback, then run a targeted KV populate for the hot prefixes and re-evaluate; detailed postmortem to follow.
[13:10] Tom Alvarez: ok that's acceptable.
[13:14] Sam Rivera: great. thanks everyone. we'll circulate notes and action items.
[13:20] Elena Kors: thanks.
[13:22] (call ends)

Post-call notes: Sam to attach runbook, cost spreadsheet, warmup script and Console screenshots; Maya to provide autoscale policy JSON and traffic generator config; Customer will confirm dry-run window and share QPS shape.
